title.narrative: Technical Support to Develop a Quality of Life (QoL) Index with Support of Quality of Life Program - The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia

description.narrative:
In today’s world, almost everything is measured, compared, benchmarked and mapped. This is particularly true in public policy where quantifying goals and outcomes are imperative. This trend has resulted in many global and urban initiatives to collect pertinent data and develop indicator metrics-based trackers as a means to monitor progress and inform future evidence-based decision making in development areas.
Discussions on how to better measure the progress of societies and their well-being and how to understand - and then sustain - Quality of Life in the future has become crucial. From the work of scholars , to different Commission Reports , to Government policies , there is a growing consensus that societies need to have better information and related policies on Quality of Life that complement economic productivity indicators. It also appears that in very few cases, Quality of Life measures have been used by policymakers or operationalized by local authorities. This has to do with the nature of this concept that is complex and multidimensional and has not been shaped by one particular definition. The essence of what this concept is about has to do with particular demographic, social, economic, cultural, political and/or geographic contexts.
As Quality of Life (QoL) concerns continue to dominate in the political agenda, it is becoming apparent that existing definitions are used in an interchangeable and sometimes confusing manner. The notion of Quality of Life touches on many aspects of life that have to do with space, social and economic factors, individual conditions and emotional situations; but there is no/little consensus on how it is measured. Furthermore, during the COVID-19 pandemic, our fundamental understanding of Quality of Life has come into question and gaps in information are evident. The pandemic affected the Quality of Life for many people in very profound ways but it has also shed light on the fact that fundamentally we don’t really understand what the key drivers of Quality of Life are and how to measure them in a concrete and consistent manner.
UN-Habitat study on Quality of Life shows that policies have been, in most cases, a by-product of many other policies without a clear method to connect initial measurements with resulting actions and demonstrable impact. Responding to the New Normal or what the World Economic Forum has called the Great Reset will require a fresh understanding on Quality of Life with a unified method, richer data and clear connection to decision-making. Yet, the preliminary assessments conducted in preparation of this project on 32 indexes measuring Quality of Life shows that none of these indices provide a direct measure from an integrated and holistic perspective, and none conclude on aggregated values, making it difficult to do appropriate ratings, and even less to measure the impact of policies and actions in a more scientific manner.
